nahhas-irab:3-3.t: The wāw is retained in the second [verb, «يولد»] and dropped in the first [«يلد»], because in the first it fell between a yāʾ and a kasra, while in the second it fell between a yāʾ and a fatḥa. «[Translator's note: the two verbs referred to are «لم يلد» and «ولم يولد», from the root و ل د.]»

nahhas-irab:4-4.t:
Ḥamza's reading is «كفوا». Hārūn the Reader claimed that Sulaymān ibn ʿAlī al-Hāshimī read «ولم يكن له كفئا أحد», and the meaning is the same, as [the poet] said: [al-Basīṭ] 597-
لا تقذفنّي بركن لا كفاء له ... وإن تأثّفك الأعداء بالرّفد
(Do not hurl at me a mighty pillar that has no equal (كفاء), even if the enemies surround you with their reinforcements.)
Likewise كفيّ, whose plural is أكفية. If you say كفوء and كفء, their plural is أكفاء. One says: "So-and-so withholds his daughters except from the أكفاء (equals)." So it is possible that كفو and كفء are two dialectal forms with one meaning, and it is possible that كفء is a lightened form of كفؤ, just as one says رسل and كتب [for رسُل and كتُب]. «كفوا» is the khabar (predicate) of يكن, and «أحد» is the ism (subject) of يكن. This is the view of most grammarians. However, Muḥammad ibn Yazīd [al-Mubarrad] held Sībawayh to be in error in his preference for making the ẓarf (adverbial / prepositional phrase) the khabar when it is placed first — for he [Sībawayh] prefers: إنّ في الدار زيدا جالسا — and he faulted him by means of this verse, because if «له» were the khabar, «كفوا» would not be put in the accusative as the khabar of يكن. Yet Sībawayh did in fact allow the ẓarf to be placed first without being the khabar, and he cited: [al-Rajaz] 598- ما دام فيهنّ فصيل حيّا (as long as a weaned young camel among them is alive) — and the poem rhymes in the accusative. There is another view on the accusative of كفو which I do not know any of the grammarians to have mentioned, namely that it is accusative as a naʿt (adjective) of an indefinite noun placed before it, and so it is put in the accusative as a ḥāl (circumstantial), just as you say:
جاءني مسرعا رجل (a man came to me hurrying), and as [the poet] said: [Majzūʾ al-Wāfir] 599- لميّة موحشا طلل (Mayya has a desolate ruin). But al-Farrāʾ mentioned that one says: ما كان ثمّ أحد نظير لزيد (there was no one there equal to Zayd), and if you place it first you say: ما كان ثمّ نظيرا لزيد أحد; and he did not mention the reason that necessitated this.

nahhas-irab:1-1.t: هُوَ is in the position of the nominative as mubtadaʾ (subject), a pronoun standing for "the matter" (ḍamīr al-ḥadīth / al-shaʾn), on the view of most of the Basrans and al-Kisāʾī, i.e., "the matter, which is the truth: Allah is One".

nahhas-irab:2-2.t:
There are six construals of it. The best is that your saying اللَّهُ is nominative as mubtadaʾ (subject), الصَّمَدُ its naʿt (adjective), and what follows it its khabar (predicate). The second view is that الصمد is the khabar. The third is that it is on the implication of a mubtadaʾ. The fourth, that it is a khabar after a khabar. The fifth, that it is a badal (substitute) for أحد. The sixth, that it is a badal for your first saying الله.
If it is asked: what is the meaning of the repetition (of الله)? The answer is that it carries magnification; such is the speech of the Arabs, as the poet said: [al-Khafīf] 592-
لا أرى الموت يسبق الموت شيء ... نغّص الموت ذا الغنى والفقيرا
(I see nothing that outstrips death; death has troubled the rich and the poor alike.)
He magnified the matter of death by repeating it and not using a pronoun for it; and similar is وَاسْتَغْفِرُوا اللَّهَ إِنَّ اللَّهَ غَفُورٌ رَحِيمٌ [al-Muzzammil: 20].
Al-Farrāʾ does not permit (هو) to be a pronoun for "the matter" unless something precedes it. This is an arbitrary imposition on the language; Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: يا مُوسى إِنَّهُ أَنَا اللَّهُ الْعَزِيزُ الْحَكِيمُ [al-Naml: 9], and إنّ (here) is at the beginning [Translator's note: the text reads «وإنّي الابتداء», apparently for «وإنّ في الابتداء»], and إنّ only enters upon a mubtadaʾ by consensus. Also, «هو», if it is not a pronoun for "the matter", is a mubtadaʾ at the beginning of the sūra. If someone asks: then to what does it refer? His proof is the ḥadīth that the Jews asked the Prophet ﷺ to describe his Lord, Mighty and Majestic, to them and give His lineage, so Allah, Mighty and Majestic, revealed: قُلْ هُوَ اللَّهُ أَحَدٌ.
Abū Jaʿfar said: I have dictated this ḥadīth so that it may be known as I heard it; there are things in it. Among them: it is from the ḥadīth of Jarīr [Translator's note: so in the text; evidently Juwaybir, as named next] from al-Ḍaḥḥāk, who did not hear from Ibn ʿAbbās. Aḥmad ibn Shuʿayb said: Juwaybir ibn Saʿīd, a Khurāsānī who narrates from al-Ḍaḥḥāk, is abandoned in ḥadīth (matrūk al-ḥadīth). And in it is Ismāʿīl ibn Ziyād, who is weak. We have mentioned it with what is in it so that it may be known. And in it is "al-Baʿlabakkī", as the Shaykh said, while the better form is "al-Baʿlī"; and this is permissible according to the Kufans, and we have explained it at His saying, Mighty and Majestic: عَلَيْها تِسْعَةَ عَشَرَ [al-Muddaththir: 30] [Translator's note: this sentence appears out of place in the text].
And al-Akhfash Saʿīd: his view is like the view of al-Farrāʾ, in that it (هو) is a pronoun for a singular (noun); «الله» is the khabar. Al-Akhfash said: «أحد» is a badal for «الله». Naṣr ibn ʿĀṣim and ʿAbd Allāh ibn Abī Isḥāq read أَحَدٌ اللَّهُ without nunation [Translator's note: the printed vowelling shows nunation; the reading described is أَحَدُ اللَّهُ], and likewise it is narrated from Abān ibn ʿUthmān; they dropped the nunation because of the meeting of two quiescent letters. Sībawayh recited: [al-Mutaqārib] 593- ولا ذاكر الله إلّا قليلا ("nor remembering Allah except a little"); and al-Farrāʾ recited: [al-Khafīf] 594-
كيف نومي على الفراش ولمّا ... تشمل الشّام غارة شعواء
تذهل الشّيخ عن بنيه وتلوي ... عن خدام العقلة العذراء
(How can I sleep on my bed when a widespread raid has not yet engulfed Syria — one that makes the old man forget his sons and lays bare the anklets of the secluded virgin?)
He means عن خدامٍ العقيلة, dropping the nunation because of the meeting of two quiescent letters, just as they read أَحَدٌ اللَّهُ. The better course is to give the nunation a vowel because of the meeting of two quiescent letters, since it is a (grammatical) mark and dropping it is ugly; and the reading of the community is more fitting.
Concerning «أحد» there are three views. Among them: أحد is in the sense of waḥad, and waḥad is in the sense of wāḥid, as the poet said: [al-Basīṭ] 595-
كأنّ رحلي وقد زال النّهار بنا ... يوم الجليل على مستأنس وحد
(As if my saddle, when the day had declined with us on the day of al-Jalīl, were upon a lone, wary wild bull.)
So the wāw was replaced by a hamza. The second view is that the original is wāḥid; the wāw was replaced by a hamza, and the (other) hamza was dropped so that two hamzas would not meet. The third view is that aḥad is in the sense of awwal (first), as you say "the day al-aḥad" — and "the day al-awwal" is heard from the Arabs.
Some of the people of reasoning said: in أحد there is a benefit that is not in واحد, because if you say "so-and-so has no one (wāḥid) who stands up to him" [Translator's note: the text reads «يا قوم» here and below, evidently for «يقوم»], it is possible that two or more stand up to him; but if you say "so-and-so has no one (aḥad) who stands up to him", it includes the meaning of one and more. Abū Jaʿfar said:
This is a mistake; there is no disagreement among the grammarians that أحد, when it is like this, only occurs in negation, as the poet said:
[al-Basīṭ] 596-
وقفت فيها أصيلا كي أسائلها ... عيّت جوابا وما بالرّبع من أحد
(I stood there in the late afternoon to question it; it was unable to answer, and there was no one in the encampment.)
But when it is in the sense of wāḥid, it occurs in affirmation. You say: "no one (aḥad) passed by us", i.e., no single one; and likewise قُلْ هُوَ اللَّهُ أَحَدٌ.
